fields.title: 1 Chronicles
fields.subtitle: Divrei HaYamim Alef, “The events of the days”
fields.description: The first half of Chronicles, the history of God’s people retold for those who came home from exile. It opens with a family tree that runs from Adam through the tribes of Israel, with Jabez’s prayer tucked among the names, and then tells the story of David: made king by all Israel, pouring out the water his warriors risked their lives to bring him, dancing as the ark comes up to Jerusalem, and hearing God’s promise, “I will make his throne firm forever.” It ends with David preparing for a temple he will never see and praying, “Everything comes from you; what we have given you came from your own hand.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 1 Chronicles?
qa.answer: The first half of Chronicles, which in Hebrew is a single book called Divrei HaYamim, “the events of the days”; the ancient Greek translation divided it in two, and the English name comes from Jerome. Its twenty-nine chapters begin with genealogies from Adam through all the tribes of Israel (1–9), then tell of the death of Saul (10) and the reign of David (11–29): his anointing by all Israel, the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, God’s covenant promise of an everlasting kingdom, and David’s preparations for the temple Solomon would build.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 and 2 Chronicles, and when?
qa.answer: The books do not name their author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited them to Ezra the scribe, and the last verses of 2 Chronicles are repeated at the start of the book of Ezra. Many scholars speak simply of “the Chronicler”, writing after the return from exile in Babylon, in the Persian period, perhaps around 400 BC, since the line of David in 1 Chronicles 3 runs several generations past Zerubbabel; some date the book earlier. Whether the same writer produced Ezra and Nehemiah is debated.

qa.question: How is Chronicles different from Samuel and Kings?
qa.answer: Chronicles retells much of the same history, often word for word, but for a different purpose and audience: the community that returned from exile with a temple but no king. It begins with Adam, leaves out most of the history of the northern kingdom and much of David’s family tragedy, such as his sin with Bathsheba and Absalom’s revolt, and adds a great deal about the ark, the temple, the priests, Levites and singers, and the prayers of kings and people. Its first readers knew Samuel and Kings; Chronicles is less a correction of them than a second witness, preaching the same history to a new generation.

qa.question: What is the prayer of Jabez?
qa.answer: A short prayer recorded in the middle of the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:9–10). Jabez, whose mother named him for the pain of his birth, “called on the God of Israel”, asking God to bless him, enlarge his border, keep his hand with him and keep him from harm, “And God gave him what he had asked.” It is one of several places in Chronicles’ lists where the book pauses to show that God hears those who call on him, as with the tribes east of the Jordan who “called out to God during the battle” (5:20).

qa.question: Why does 1 Chronicles 21 say that Satan moved David to count Israel?
qa.answer: In 1 Chronicles 21:1, “Satan rose up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel,” while the parallel in 2 Samuel 24:1 says that the anger of the LORD stirred David up. Many interpreters see two sides of one event, God permitting what the adversary intended, as in the opening of Job; some note that the Hebrew word has no article and may mean simply “an adversary”. Both accounts hold David responsible, and in both he confesses his sin. Chronicles goes on to show the place of his repentance, Ornan’s threshing floor, becoming the site of the temple.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name, and the psalm of chapter 16 is set out line by line as poetry. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
To you, LORD, belong the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory and the majesty; indeed everything in heaven and on earth is yours. The kingdom is yours, LORD, and you are lifted high as head over all.

— 1 Chronicles 29:11

No book of the Bible begins less promisingly. 1 Chronicles opens with three names, “Adam, Seth, Enosh,” and goes on listing names for nine chapters. Many readers stop there. That is a pity, because the lists are a door, and behind them is one of the most joyful books in the Old Testament: a book about worship, about prayer, and about a people learning who they are after they had lost almost everything.

Its Hebrew name is Divrei HaYamim, “the events of the days”, the ordinary phrase for a court’s annals. The ancient Greek translators called it Paraleipomena, “things left out”, because they took it to supply what Samuel and Kings had passed over; the name Chronicles comes from Jerome, who suggested it be called a chronicle of the whole of sacred history. Like Samuel and Kings it was one book in Hebrew, divided in two by the Greek translation. 1 Chronicles runs from Adam to the death of David; 2 Chronicles from Solomon to the decree that sent the exiles home. In most Hebrew Bibles it stands last of all, so that the Hebrew Scriptures end with a king’s invitation to go up to Jerusalem.

A book for people after the exile

To understand Chronicles, start with its first readers. It was written after the return from Babylon: David’s family tree in chapter 3 runs several generations past Zerubbabel, who led exiles home after Cyrus’s decree and rebuilt the temple around 520–515 BC, and chapter 9 lists “the first to settle again on their own property in their towns”. Its readers were a small community in a corner of the Persian Empire. They had a rebuilt temple, smaller than Solomon’s, and no king. They had every reason to wonder whether the promises still applied to them.

Chronicles answers by retelling their story, mostly from Samuel and Kings, but with its own emphases and many additions. Its message is that they are still “all Israel”, still the people of the God who chose David and Jerusalem; that the worship of the temple is the heart of their life; and that the God who answered prayer in David’s day still answers those who seek him. It is not a second, inferior copy of Samuel and Kings. It is a sermon on that history for a new generation.

A family tree from Adam

The genealogies of chapters 1–9 are a map of who belongs. They begin with the whole human race, “Adam, Seth, Enosh”, narrow to Abraham and then to “the sons of Israel”, and then go tribe by tribe through nearly all of them (only Dan and Zebulun get no genealogy). Judah, David’s tribe, comes first and gets the most space; Levi, the tribe of priests and temple singers, stands at the centre; and the northern tribes, long since scattered by Assyria, are included too. Chronicles will not write anyone out of Israel.

Christian readers will recognise the method. The New Testament opens the same way, with “The record of the family line of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and Luke traces that line back, as Chronicles does, to Adam. A genealogy is a way of saying that God has been keeping his promises through every generation, including the ones nobody remembers.

Scattered among the names are small stories, like flowers in a stone wall. A man of Judah named Jabez, whose mother named him for the pain of his birth, prays a short prayer:

Jabez called on the God of Israel: “If only you would bless me richly and enlarge my border! If only your hand would be with me, and you would keep me from harm, so that it might not pain me!” And God gave him what he had asked.

— 1 Chronicles 4:10

Some tribes east of the Jordan win a battle “because they called out to God during the battle, and he answered their prayer, since they trusted in him”. A family of potters “made their home there with the king, working for him.” The men of Issachar were “men with insight into the times, who knew what Israel ought to do” (12:32). Even the lists keep saying the book’s great themes: God hears those who call on him, and the humblest work done for the King matters.

Saul, and the word “seek”

The story proper begins with Saul’s last battle, told in a single chapter, and a verdict:

He did not seek the LORD. So the LORD put him to death and handed the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.

— 1 Chronicles 10:14

“Seek” is one of the key words of Chronicles. Saul did not seek the LORD, and asked a medium for guidance instead. David brings the ark back because, as he says, “we did not seek it in the days of Saul.” David tells Solomon, “If you seek him, he will let you find him” (28:9), and the theme runs on through 2 Chronicles. To seek the LORD, in this book, means to turn to him in worship and prayer, to ask his will, and to rely on him rather than anything else.

David, king of all Israel

In chapter 11 “all Israel” gathers to David at Hebron, “we are your own bone and flesh,” and anoints him king. He takes Jerusalem, and Chronicles lists the mighty warriors who stood with him. One story among them shows the kind of king he was. Hiding from the Philistines, David longs aloud for water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem, his home town; three of his men break through the enemy camp to bring it. He will not drink it. He pours it out as an offering to the LORD: “Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives?”

Men come over to David from every tribe, and the Spirit comes on one of their leaders, Amasai, who cries out, “We are yours, David! We are with you, son of Jesse!” Chapter 12 ends with a feast at Hebron and the people’s neighbours bringing food on donkeys and camels, “For there was joy in Israel.” Joy is another of the book’s words.

The ark comes home

David’s first act as king of all Israel is to bring the ark of the covenant, the sign of God’s presence, to Jerusalem. The first attempt ends in disaster. The ark is carried on a cart, the oxen stumble, and Uzzah puts out his hand to steady it: “Then the anger of the LORD blazed against Uzzah, and he struck him down.” David is angry and afraid. The ark stays three months in the house of Obed-Edom, and that house is blessed.

The story is hard, and Chronicles does not soften it. But it draws a lesson: the holy God is not to be handled as a possession. When David tries again, the ark is carried by Levites, as the law of Moses required, and David admits, “we did not seek him as the rule required.” This time it comes up to Jerusalem with shouts, trumpets, harps and lyres, and with the king dancing before it.

Then David appoints Levites “to invoke, to thank and to praise the LORD”, and gives them a psalm. It is woven from parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106, and it is the first song of the new order of worship in Jerusalem:

Give the LORD thanks, for he is good; his loyal love lasts forever.

— 1 Chronicles 16:34

That refrain will be heard again and again in Chronicles, at the dedication of the temple and on the battlefield. For people who had lost their king, it was a reminder of what they had not lost.

“The LORD will build you a house”

Chapter 17 is the theological heart of the book. Settled in his palace, David is troubled that the ark of the LORD “stays under tent curtains”, and he proposes to build it a temple. That night God sends Nathan the prophet with a reversal. David will not build a house for God; God will build a house, a dynasty, for David: “I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.” One of David’s sons will build the temple, and of him God says:

I will keep him in place over my house and my kingdom forever, and his throne will stand firm for all time.’”

— 1 Chronicles 17:14

Set it beside the same promise in 2 Samuel 7:16, where God says to David, “Your house and your kingdom will be secure forever before you.” Chronicles has “my house and my kingdom”. The kingdom of Israel belongs to God; its king sits, as Chronicles later says, “on the throne of the LORD” (29:23). For readers who had no king, that was the point: the kingdom had never really been David’s, and so it could not die with David’s dynasty. Christians have heard in it the promise that the angel would repeat to Mary, that her son would be given “the throne of David” and that “There will be no end to his kingdom” (Luke 1:32–33).

David’s answer is wonder: “LORD God, who am I, and what is my house, that you have brought me as far as this?”

What Chronicles leaves out

Readers who know 2 Samuel notice what is missing. Bathsheba appears only once, as a name in a list (3:5, where she is called Bathshua). There is no murder of Uriah, no Nathan saying “You are the man!”, no story of Amnon or Absalom, no long years of family tragedy. Some have accused the Chronicler of whitewashing his hero. But his first readers had the books of Samuel and knew the story well. He was not hiding it; he was telling a different part of it, the David who gathered Israel, brought the ark home and prepared for the temple. Like the four Gospels, the Old Testament gives more than one witness to its history, each with its own purpose.

And Chronicles does not pretend David was sinless. It tells, in full, the sin that brought the most suffering on the people.

The census and the threshing floor

“Satan rose up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel.” The parallel in 2 Samuel 24:1 says that the anger of the LORD “stirred David up”. Readers have long discussed the difference. Many see two sides of one event: God permitting what the adversary intended, as in the book of Job. Some note that the Hebrew word here has no article and may mean simply “an adversary”. Either way, David is held responsible, and he says so: “I have sinned greatly by doing this.”

Given a choice of punishments, he answers, “Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great.” When the plague falls, he pleads for the people: “It is I who have sinned and done great wrong. But these sheep, what have they done?” He is told to build an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, and he insists on paying full price: “I will not take what is yours for the LORD, or offer a burnt offering at no cost to myself.” Fire falls from heaven on the altar. And David declares, “Here is the house of the LORD God.” The place of his sin and God’s mercy becomes the site of the temple, on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1), the name of the land where Abraham once offered Isaac (Genesis 22:2).

Preparing for a temple he would not build

The last eight chapters show David spending the end of his life on a building he will never see. He is not allowed to build it, because he has “poured out blood”; the builder will be Solomon, “a man of rest”, whose name sounds like the Hebrew word for peace. So David gathers materials, organises the priests and Levites into divisions, appoints gatekeepers, treasurers and officials, and sets apart singers “who prophesied with lyres, harps and cymbals”. Their task is to stand “each morning to give thanks and praise to the LORD, and to do the same in the evening”. Long lists again, but lists of people whose work was worship.

Then David hands Solomon the plans, “in writing from the hand of the LORD upon me”, and a charge: “Be strong and courageous, and do the work.” He gives his own treasure, and asks the people, “who is willing to give freely and consecrate themselves today to the LORD?” They give gladly, “for with a whole heart they had given freely to the LORD.”

The book ends with David’s last prayer, which begins with the verse at the head of this introduction and turns, at its centre, on a question every giver should ask: “But who am I, and who are my people, that we should have the means to give as freely as this? Everything comes from you; what we have given you came from your own hand.” Then David dies “at a good old age, having had his fill of days, riches and honor”, and Solomon sits on the throne of the LORD.

How to read 1 Chronicles

Do not be afraid to read chapters 1–9 quickly, watching for their shape and for the small stories in them; then slow down for David. It helps to read the narrative beside 2 Samuel and notice what Chronicles adds, especially its long attention to the ark, the Levites and the music of worship. Psalms 96, 105 and 106 are worth reading with chapter 16. If you have time for only two chapters, read 17 and 29: the promise to David, and David’s prayer at the end of his life.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited it to Ezra, and the end of 2 Chronicles repeats the opening of the book of Ezra. Many scholars speak simply of “the Chronicler”, writing in the Persian period, perhaps around 400 BC; some date it earlier, and whether the same hand wrote Ezra and Nehemiah is debated. The writer names his sources, among them “the records of Samuel the seer, the records of Nathan the prophet and the records of Gad the seer”. Some of his numbers differ from those in Samuel and Kings, through copying or different ways of counting, and Christians hold a range of views on the details.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Chronicles are worth knowing.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation follows long custom and writes “the LORD”. The title older translations give as “the LORD of hosts” appears as “the LORD of Armies”.

“Loyal love.” The Hebrew word hesed, God’s steadfast covenant love, is “loyal love” in the great refrain “his loyal love lasts forever”, and “faithful love” in the promise to David’s son.

Seeking. The Hebrew verbs for seeking God are usually rendered “seek”, but in the psalm of chapter 16 the line older translations give as “seek his face continually” becomes “come into his presence again and again”, which is what it means. That psalm, like the other poetry in the book, is printed line by line.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 1
fields.body_html:
From Adam to Abraham

Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Ham and Japheth.

The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras.

The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Diphath and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittim and the Rodanim.

The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

Cush was the father of Nimrod, who became the first great warrior on the earth.

Egypt was the ancestor of the Ludites, the Anamites, the Lehabites, the Naphtuhites, the Pathrusites, the Casluhites (from whom the Philistines came) and the Caphtorites.

Canaan was the father of Sidon, his firstborn, and of Heth, and of the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites and the Hamathites.

The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech.

Arpachshad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber. Two sons were born to Eber. One was named Peleg, because in his time the earth was divided. His brother was named Joktan. Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab. All these were sons of Joktan.

Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abram, that is, Abraham.

The descendants of Abraham

The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael.

This is their family line: Nebaioth, Ishmael’s firstborn, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah. These were the sons of Ishmael.

The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan.

The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah. All these were Keturah’s descendants.

Abraham was the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.

The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam and Korah.

The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna and Amalek.

The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah.

The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam. Lotan’s sister was Timna.

The sons of Shobal: Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. The sons of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran.

The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan and Jaakan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.

The kings and chiefs of Edom

These are the kings who ruled the land of Edom before any king ruled over the Israelites: Bela son of Beor, whose city was named Dinhabah. When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah, became king in his place. When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king in his place. When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad became king in his place; he was the one who defeated Midian in the country of Moab. His city was named Avith. When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became king in his place. When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River became king in his place. When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor became king in his place. When Baal-hanan died, Hadad became king in his place. His city was named Pai, and his wife was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab. Then Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel and Iram. These were the chiefs of Edom.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 2
fields.body_html:
The sons of Israel

These were the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad and Asher.

The descendants of Judah

The sons of Judah: Er, Onan and Shelah. Bath-shua, a Canaanite woman, was the mother of these three. But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was evil in the LORD’s eyes, and he brought his life to an end.

His daughter-in-law Tamar bore him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.

The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.

The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara, five in all.

The son of Carmi: Achar, the one who brought trouble on Israel by breaking faith over the devoted things.

The son of Ethan: Azariah. The sons born to Hezron: Jerahmeel, Ram and Chelubai. Ram was the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, the leader of the people of Judah. Nahshon was the father of Salma, and Salma was the father of Boaz. Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse. Jesse was the father of Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third, Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth, Ozem the sixth and David the seventh. Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab and Asahel, three of them. Abigail bore Amasa, and Amasa’s father was Jether the Ishmaelite. Caleb son of Hezron had children by Azubah his wife and by Jerioth. Her sons were Jesher, Shobab and Ardon. When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, and she bore him Hur. Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel.

Later Hezron lay with the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he took as his wife at the age of sixty. She bore him Segub. Segub was the father of Jair, who had twenty-three towns in the land of Gilead. But Geshur and Aram took Havvoth-jair from them, with Kenath and its villages, sixty towns. All these were descendants of Machir the father of Gilead. After Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah, his wife Abijah bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa. The sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron: Ram the firstborn, then Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. Jerahmeel had another wife, named Atarah. She was the mother of Onam.

The sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin and Eker. The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur. Abishur’s wife was named Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid. The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim. Seled died without sons.

The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The descendant of Sheshan: Ahlai. The sons of Jada the brother of Shammai: Jether and Jonathan. Jether died without sons.

The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel. Sheshan had no sons, only daughters. But Sheshan had an Egyptian servant named Jarha. Sheshan gave his daughter as a wife to his servant Jarha, and she bore him Attai. Attai was the father of Nathan, and Nathan was the father of Zabad. Zabad was the father of Ephlal, and Ephlal was the father of Obed. Obed was the father of Jehu, and Jehu was the father of Azariah. Azariah was the father of Helez, and Helez was the father of Eleasah. Eleasah was the father of Sismai, and Sismai was the father of Shallum. Shallum was the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah was the father of Elishama. The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mesha his firstborn, who was the father of Ziph, and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron. The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. Shema was the father of Raham the father of Jorkeam, and Rekem was the father of Shammai. The son of Shammai: Maon, and Maon was the father of Beth-zur. Ephah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Haran, Moza and Gazez. Haran was the father of Gazez.

The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph. Maacah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah. She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, and Sheva the father of Machbenah and of Gibea. Caleb’s daughter was Achsah.

These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim, Salma the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader. Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had descendants: Haroeh, half of the Manahathites. The clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites and the Mishraites. From these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.

The descendants of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, half of the Manahathites, and the Zorites. The clans of scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Sucathites. These were the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 3
fields.body_html:
The sons of David

The sons born to David in Hebron were these: the firstborn, Amnon, whose mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel; the second, Daniel, whose mother was Abigail of Carmel; the third was Absalom, whose mother was Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; the fourth was Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, whose mother was Abital; the sixth was Ithream, whose mother was Eglah his wife. Six sons were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. In Jerusalem he reigned for thirty-three years.

These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, the four sons whose mother was Bathshua daughter of Ammiel; and Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada and Eliphelet: nine sons. All these were sons of David, besides the sons of his concubines; and Tamar was their sister.

The kings of Judah and their descendants

The son of Solomon was Rehoboam; Abijah was his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son, Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son, Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son, Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son, Amon his son, Josiah his son. The sons of Josiah: the firstborn was Johanan, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum. The sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son. The sons of Jeconiah the captive: Shealtiel his son, and Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah. The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and their sister was Shelomith, and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-Hesed: five sons. The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah; the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah.

The sons of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. The sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat: six. The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah and Azrikam: three. The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah and Anani: seven.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 4
fields.body_html:
More descendants of Judah

The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur and Shobal. Reaiah son of Shobal was the father of Jahath, and Jahath was the father of Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites.

These were the sons of the father of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma and Idbash. Their sister was named Hazzelelponi. Penuel was the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah and the father of Bethlehem. Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah. Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah. The sons of Helah: Zereth, Zohar and Ethnan. Koz was the father of Anub and Zobebah, and of the clans of Aharhel son of Harum. Jabez was held in greater honor than his brothers. His mother gave him the name Jabez, for she said, “I bore him in pain.” Jabez called on the God of Israel: “If only you would bless me richly and enlarge my border! If only your hand would be with me, and you would keep me from harm, so that it might not pain me!” And God gave him what he had asked. Chelub the brother of Shuhah was the father of Mehir, who was the father of Eshton. Eshton was the father of Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Ir-nahash. These were the men of Recah.

The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah. The sons of Othniel: Hathath. Meonothai was the father of Ophrah. Seraiah was the father of Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, the Valley of Craftsmen, for its people were craftsmen.

The sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah and Naam. The sons of Elah: Kenaz. The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria and Asarel. The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher and Jalon. She conceived Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa. His Judean wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. These are the sons of Bithiah, Pharaoh’s daughter, whom Mered married.

The sons of Hodiah’s wife, the sister of Naham, were the father of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite. The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth. The sons of Shelah son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, the clans of the guild of linen workers at Beth-ashbea, and Jokim, the men of Cozeba, Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab, and Jashubi-lehem. These records are ancient. They were potters, and they lived in Netaim and Gederah; they made their home there with the king, working for him.

The descendants of Simeon

The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah and Shaul. Shaul’s son was Shallum, his son was Mibsam, and his son was Mishma. The descendants of Mishma: his son Hammuel, Hammuel’s son Zaccur, and Zaccur’s son Shimei. Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brothers had few children, and their whole clan did not become as numerous as the people of Judah.

They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad, Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri and Shaaraim. These were their towns until the reign of David. Their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen and Ashan, five towns, and all their villages around these towns as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept their own genealogical record. Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah son of Amaziah, Joel, Jehu son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel, Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, and Ziza son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah. These men listed by name were leaders in their clans, and their ancestral families grew very large. They went to the approach to Gedor, as far as the east side of the valley, looking for pasture for their flocks. They found rich, good pasture, and the land was wide open, quiet and at peace, for those who had lived there before were descended from Ham. In the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, these men whose names are written here came and attacked their tents and the Meunites who were found there. They devoted them to destruction, so that they are gone to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks. Some of them, five hundred men of Simeon, went to Mount Seir, led by Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi. They struck down the Amalekites who were left, those who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 5
fields.body_html:
The descendants of Reuben

The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel—he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father’s bed, his birthright went to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, and the genealogy is not set out according to the birthright; for Judah grew stronger than his brothers, and a ruler came from him, though the birthright belonged to Joseph—

the sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. The descendants of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son, Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son, and Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria took away into exile. He was a leader of the Reubenites. His relatives by their clans, as their generations were recorded in the genealogy, were Jeiel the chief, Zechariah, and Bela son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel. He lived in Aroer and as far as Nebo and Baal-meon. To the east he settled as far as the edge of the desert that stretches from the Euphrates River, because their herds had grown large in the land of Gilead. In the days of Saul they made war on the Hagrites, who fell into their power, and they lived in their tents across the whole region east of Gilead.

The descendants of Gad

The Gadites lived next to them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah. Joel was the chief, Shapham the second, then Janai and Shaphat in Bashan. Their relatives by their ancestral families were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven in all.

These were the sons of Abihail son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz. Ahi son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was head of their ancestral family. They lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its villages, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their farthest edges. All of them were entered in the genealogies while Jotham was king of Judah and Jeroboam was king of Israel.

The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh had capable warriors, men who carried shield and sword, drew the bow and were trained for war: 44,760 who could go out to war. They made war on the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish and Nodab. They received help against them, and the Hagrites and everyone with them were handed over to them, because they called out to God during the battle, and he answered their prayer, since they trusted in him. They captured their livestock, 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep and 2,000 donkeys, and they took 100,000 people captive. Many fell dead, because the war was God’s doing. And they lived in their place until the exile.

The half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan

The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They grew numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir and Mount Hermon. These were the heads of their ancestral families: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel. All of them were mighty warriors and famous men, heads of their ancestral families. But they were unfaithful to the God of their ancestors and gave themselves like prostitutes to the gods of the peoples of the land, peoples God had destroyed before them. So the God of Israel stirred the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, that is, of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he carried them into exile, the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. He took them to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river of Gozan, and they remain there to this day.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 6
fields.body_html:
The line of the high priests

The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath and Merari. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel.

The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.

Eleazar was the father of Phinehas, and Phinehas was the father of Abishua. Abishua was the father of Bukki, and Bukki was the father of Uzzi. Uzzi was the father of Zerahiah, and Zerahiah was the father of Meraioth. Meraioth was the father of Amariah, and Amariah was the father of Ahitub. Ahitub was the father of Zadok, and Zadok was the father of Ahimaaz. Ahimaaz was the father of Azariah, and Azariah was the father of Johanan. Johanan was the father of Azariah. It was he who was priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. Azariah was the father of Amariah, and Amariah was the father of Ahitub. Ahitub was the father of Zadok, and Zadok was the father of Shallum. Shallum was the father of Hilkiah, and Hilkiah was the father of Azariah. Azariah was the father of Seraiah, and Seraiah was the father of Jehozadak.

The descendants of Levi

Jehozadak went into exile when the LORD exiled Judah and Jerusalem through Nebuchadnezzar.

The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath and Merari. These are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites, by their ancestral families. From Gershom: Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son, Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, Jeatherai his son. The descendants of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son, Elkanah his son, Ebiasaph his son, Assir his son, Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son and Shaul his son. The sons of Elkanah: Amasai and Ahimoth. Elkanah: the sons of Elkanah were Zophai his son and Nahath his son, Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son. The sons of Samuel: Vashni the firstborn, and Abijah.

The descendants of Merari: Mahli, Libni his son, Shimei his son, Uzzah his son, Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son.

The singers David appointed

These are the men David put in charge of the singing in the house of the LORD after the ark had come to rest. Until Solomon built the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, they ministered with song before the tabernacle of the tent of meeting, carrying out their service in the order laid down for them. These are the men who served, with their sons. From the Kohathites: Heman the singer, son of Joel, son of Samuel, son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Toah, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel. His kinsman Asaph stood at his right hand: Asaph son of Berechiah, son of Shimea, son of Michael, son of Baaseiah, son of Malchijah, son of Ethni, son of Zerah, son of Adaiah, son of Ethan, son of Zimmah, son of Shimei, son of Jahath, son of Gershom, son of Levi.

On the left were their kinsmen, the descendants of Merari: Ethan son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch, son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah, son of Amzi, son of Bani, son of Shemer, son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi.

Their fellow Levites were appointed to all the service of the tabernacle, the house of God. But Aaron and his sons made the offerings go up in smoke on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense. They did all the work of the Most Holy Place and made atonement for Israel, just as Moses the servant of God had commanded.

These are the descendants of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son, Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son, Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son, Zadok his son, Ahimaaz his son.

The towns of the Levites

These are the places where they lived, their settlements within their territory. To the descendants of Aaron, of the clan of the Kohathites, the lot fell. They gave them Hebron in the land of Judah, and its pasturelands around it. But the fields of the town and its villages they had given to Caleb son of Jephunneh.

To the descendants of Aaron they gave one of the cities of refuge, Hebron, along with Libnah and its pasturelands, Jattir, and Eshtemoa and its pasturelands, Hilez and its pasturelands, Debir and its pasturelands, Ashan and its pasturelands, and Beth-shemesh and its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Geba and its pasturelands, Alemeth and its pasturelands, and Anathoth and its pasturelands. Their towns numbered thirteen in all, clan by clan.

The rest of the descendants of Kohath received ten towns by lot from the clan of the tribe and from the half-tribe of Manasseh.

The descendants of Gershom, clan by clan, received thirteen towns from the tribes of Issachar, Asher and Naphtali and from the tribe of Manasseh in Bashan.

The descendants of Merari, clan by clan, received twelve towns by lot from the tribes of Reuben, Gad and Zebulun. So the Israelites gave the Levites the towns and their pasturelands. From the tribes of Judah, Simeon and Benjamin they gave by lot these towns, which are mentioned by name.

As for some of the clans of the descendants of Kohath, the towns of their territory came from the tribe of Ephraim. They gave them one of the cities of refuge, Shechem and its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, along with Gezer and its pasturelands, Jokmeam and its pasturelands, Beth-horon and its pasturelands, Aijalon and its pasturelands, and Gath-rimmon and its pasturelands.

From the half-tribe of Manasseh they gave Aner and its pasturelands, and Bileam and its pasturelands. These went to the clan of the rest of the descendants of Kohath.

To the descendants of Gershom they gave, from the clan of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Golan in Bashan and its pasturelands, and Ashtaroth and its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Issachar they gave Kedesh and its pasturelands, Daberath and its pasturelands, Ramoth and its pasturelands, and Anem and its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Asher they gave Mashal and its pasturelands, Abdon and its pasturelands, Hukok and its pasturelands, and Rehob and its pasturelands. From the tribe of Naphtali they gave Kedesh in Galilee and its pasturelands, Hammon and its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim and its pasturelands.

To the descendants of Merari, the remaining Levites, they gave from the tribe of Zebulun Rimmono and its pasturelands, and Tabor and its pasturelands. Across the Jordan from Jericho, on the east side of the Jordan, they gave from the tribe of Reuben Bezer in the wilderness and its pasturelands, Jahaz and its pasturelands, Kedemoth and its pasturelands, and Mephaath and its pasturelands. From the tribe of Gad they gave Ramoth in Gilead and its pasturelands, Mahanaim and its pasturelands, Heshbon and its pasturelands, and Jazer and its pasturelands.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 7
fields.body_html:
The descendants of Issachar

The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub and Shimron, four in all.

The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam and Shemuel. They were heads of their ancestral families descended from Tola, mighty warriors listed by their generations. In the days of David they numbered 22,600.

The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. The sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel and Isshiah. All five of them were chiefs. Along with them, by their generations and ancestral families, there were 36,000 troops ready for war, for they had many wives and children. Their relatives in all the clans of Issachar were mighty warriors. In all, 87,000 of them were registered in the genealogies.

The descendants of Benjamin

The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher and Jediael, three in all. The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri, five in all. They were heads of ancestral families, mighty warriors, and 22,034 were registered in their genealogies.

The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher. Registered in their genealogies by their generations, as heads of their ancestral families, were 20,200 mighty warriors.

The son of Jediael: Bilhan. The sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish and Ahishahar. All these were sons of Jediael, listed by the heads of their families: 17,200 mighty warriors ready to go out to war. Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, and Hushim was the son of Aher. The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum. These were descendants of Bilhah.

The descendants of Manasseh

The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his wife bore, and Machir the father of Gilead, whom his Aramean concubine bore. Machir took a wife for Huppim and Shuppim, and his sister’s name was Maacah. The second was named Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters. Maacah, the wife of Machir, gave birth to a son, and she named him Peresh. His brother’s name was Sheresh, and his sons were Ulam and Rekem. The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the descendants of Gilead son of Machir, son of Manasseh. His sister Hammolecheth gave birth to Ishhod, Abiezer and Mahlah. The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi and Aniam.

The descendants of Ephraim

The descendants of Ephraim: Shuthelah, Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son, Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and also Ezer and Elead. The men of Gath who were born in that land killed Ezer and Elead, because they went down to take their livestock. Ephraim their father mourned for many days, and his relatives came to console him. Then he lay with his wife, and she became pregnant and bore a son. He named him Beriah, because disaster had come upon his family. His daughter was Sheerah. She built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and also Uzzen-sheerah. Rephah was his son, and also Resheph; then Telah his son, Tahan his son, Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son, Nun his son and Joshua his son. Their land and settlements were Bethel with its villages, Naaran on the east, Gezer with its villages on the west, and Shechem with its villages as far as Ayyah with its villages. Along the borders of the descendants of Manasseh were Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor, each with its villages. The descendants of Joseph son of Israel made their homes in these towns.

The descendants of Asher

The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi and Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel, who was the father of Birzaith. Heber was the father of Japhlet, Shomer and Hotham, and of their sister Shua. The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal and Ashvath. These were the sons of Japhlet. The sons of Shemer: Ahi, Rohgah, Hubbah and Aram. The sons of his brother Helem: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh and Amal. The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran and Beera. The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa and Ara. The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel and Rizia. All these were descendants of Asher, heads of ancestral families, choice men, mighty warriors, chief among the leaders. The number of men registered in their genealogies for service in war was 26,000.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 8
fields.body_html:
More descendants of Benjamin

Benjamin was the father of Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third, Nohah the fourth and Rapha the fifth.

Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Gera, Shephuphan and Huram. These were the sons of Ehud, who were heads of families among those living in Geba and who were taken away into exile to Manahath: Naaman, Ahijah and Gera. Gera was the one who took them into exile, and he was the father of Uzzah and Ahihud. Shaharaim had sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away his wives Hushim and Baara. By his wife Hodesh he was the father of Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of families. By Hushim he had been the father of Abitub and Elpaal. The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham and Shemed; he built Ono, and Lod with the villages around it. Beriah and Shema were heads of families among those who lived in Aijalon, and they drove out the people of Gath. Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad, Eder, Michael, Ishpah and Joha were the sons of Beriah. Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal. Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei. Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah and Penuel were the sons of Shashak. Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaareshiah, Elijah and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham. These were heads of families, listed by their generations, and they were leading men. They lived in Jerusalem.

The father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and his wife’s name was Maacah. His firstborn son was Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio and Zecher. Mikloth was the father of Shimeah. These also lived near their relatives in Jerusalem, alongside their kinsmen.

The family of Saul

Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malki-Shua, Abinadab and Esh-baal. The son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.

The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea and Ahaz. Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah, Jehoaddah was the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri, and Zimri was the father of Moza. Moza was the father of Binea; Binea’s son was Raphah, his son Eleasah, and his son Azel. Azel had six sons, whose names were Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. All of these were Azel’s sons. The sons of his brother Eshek: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second and Eliphelet the third. The sons of Ulam were mighty warriors, skilled archers. They had many sons and grandsons, 150 altogether. All these belonged to the descendants of Benjamin.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 9
fields.body_html:
All Israel was enrolled by genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. Judah was taken into exile to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness.

The first to settle again in their towns

The first to settle again on their own property in their towns were Israelites, priests, Levites and temple servants. Some of the descendants of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem: From Judah: Uthai son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, a descendant of Perez son of Judah. From the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn and his sons. From the descendants of Zerah: Jeuel. Their relatives numbered 690. From the descendants of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah, Ibneiah son of Jeroham; Elah son of Uzzi, son of Michri; and Meshullam son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah, and their relatives, listed by their family records, numbered 956. All these men were heads of families in their ancestral houses.

The priests

From the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, Azariah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God,

Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah; Maasai son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer; and their relatives, heads of their ancestral families, 1,760 in all. They were very capable men for the work of serving in the house of God. From the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, a descendant of Merari; Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal; Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph; Obadiah son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun; and Berechiah son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites. The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon and Ahiman. Their kinsman Shallum was the chief, and to this day he is stationed at the King’s Gate on the east. These were the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites. Shallum son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his relatives from his father’s family, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service as keepers of the thresholds of the tent, just as their ancestors had been in charge of the camp of the LORD as keepers of the entrance. Phinehas son of Eleazar had been in charge of them in earlier times, and the LORD was with him. Zechariah son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance to the tent of meeting. All those chosen to be gatekeepers at the thresholds numbered 212. They were enrolled by genealogy in their villages. It was David and Samuel the seer who had placed them in these posts of trust. So they and their descendants were in charge of guarding the gates of the house of the LORD, the house that was the tent. The gatekeepers were on all four sides: east, west, north and south. Their relatives in their villages had to come in from time to time to serve with them for seven days. For the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, held a permanent position of trust. They were in charge of the rooms and the treasuries of the house of God. They spent the night stationed around the house of God, because they had the duty of guarding it, and they were in charge of the key for opening it every morning. Some of them were in charge of the utensils used in the service; they counted them when they brought them in and when they took them out. Others were appointed over the furnishings and all the holy utensils of the sanctuary, and over the fine flour, wine, oil, frankincense and spices. But some of the priests prepared the blend of the spices. Mattithiah, one of the Levites and the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with baking the flat cakes. Some of their relatives, the Kohathites, were in charge of the bread set out in rows, preparing it every Sabbath.

These are the singers, heads of Levite families, who stayed in the temple rooms and were excused from other tasks, because they were at their work day and night. These were heads of Levite families, leaders listed in their family records, and they lived in Jerusalem.

Saul’s family again

Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and his wife’s name was Maacah. His firstborn son was Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah and Mikloth. Mikloth was the father of Shimeam. They also lived near their relatives in Jerusalem, alongside their kinsmen.

Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malki-Shua, Abinadab and Esh-baal. The son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal was the father of Micah. The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech and Tahrea. Ahaz was the father of Jarah, Jarah was the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri, and Zimri was the father of Moza. Moza was the father of Binea; Binea’s son was Rephaiah, his son Eleasah, and his son Azel. Azel had six sons, whose names were Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. These were Azel’s sons.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 10
fields.body_html:
The death of Saul

Now the Philistines fought against Israel. The men of Israel fled from the Philistines, and many fell dead on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines caught up with Saul and his sons, and they killed Jonathan, Abinadab and Malki-Shua, Saul’s sons. The fighting pressed hard against Saul. The archers found him with their bows, and he was wounded by them. Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, or these uncircumcised men will come and make sport of me.” But his armor-bearer would not do it, because he was terrified. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it. Seeing that Saul was dead, his armor-bearer also fell on his own sword and died.

So Saul and his three sons died, and his whole house died together. All the men of Israel who lived in the valley saw that the army was in flight and that Saul and his sons had died. So they abandoned their towns and fled, and the Philistines came and settled in them.

On the next day the Philistines came to strip the dead, and they found Saul and his sons lying where they had fallen on Mount Gilboa. They stripped Saul and carried off his head and his armor, and they sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people. They placed his armor in the temple of their gods, and in the temple of Dagon they fastened up his head.

All the people of Jabesh-gilead heard everything the Philistines had done to Saul. All their brave men set out, took away the bodies of Saul and his sons, and carried them to Jabesh. They buried their bones under the terebinth tree in Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days. So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD. He did not keep the word of the LORD, and he also asked a medium for guidance. He did not seek the LORD. So the LORD put him to death and handed the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 11
fields.body_html:
David becomes king over all Israel

Then all Israel gathered to David in Hebron. “Look,” they told him, “we are your own bone and flesh. In times past, even while Saul reigned, you were the one who led Israel out to battle and brought them back. And the LORD your God said to you, ‘You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel; you will become ruler over my people Israel.’” When all the elders of Israel had come to the king in Hebron, David made a covenant with them there in the presence of the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel, as the LORD had promised through Samuel.

David captures Jerusalem

Then David and all Israel marched on Jerusalem, that is, Jebus, where the Jebusites lived, the people of that land. The people of Jebus told David, “You will not get in here.” But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is now the City of David. David had said, “Whoever is first to strike down a Jebusite will become chief and commander.” Joab son of Zeruiah went up first, so he became chief. David took up residence in the stronghold, and that is why it was called the City of David. He built up the city all around, from the Millo to the area around it, and Joab repaired the rest of the city. David became greater and greater, for the LORD of Armies was with him.

David’s mighty warriors

These are the chiefs of David’s mighty warriors, who gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, as the LORD had promised concerning Israel.

This is the roll of David’s mighty warriors. Jashobeam son of Hachmoni was chief of the Thirty. He raised his spear against three hundred men and killed them at one time. Next to him was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. He was one of the three mighty warriors. He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines had gathered there for battle. There was a plot of land full of barley, and the troops ran from the Philistines. But they took their stand in the middle of the plot, defended it and struck down the Philistines, and the LORD saved them with a great victory. Once three chief men of the Thirty went down to the rock, to join David at the cave of Adullam, while an army of Philistines was camped in the Valley of Rephaim. At that time David was in the stronghold, and a Philistine garrison was then in Bethlehem. David had a longing and said, “If only someone would get me water to drink from Bethlehem’s well, the one by the gate!” So the three men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, and carried it back to David. But David would not drink it. Instead he poured it out as an offering to the LORD. He said, “Before my God, far be it from me to do this! Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives? For they risked their lives to bring it.” So he would not drink it. Such were the deeds of the three mighty warriors. Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the Three. He raised his spear against three hundred men and killed them, and he won a name alongside the Three. He was doubly honored above the Three and became their commander, but he did not reach the rank of the Three.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada was the son of a brave man from Kabzeel who did great deeds. He struck down the two champions of Moab. He also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion. He also struck down an Egyptian, a man of great height, about 7 1/2 feet tall. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand like a weaver’s beam, but Benaiah went down against him with a club, snatched the spear from the Egyptian’s grip and killed him with his own weapon. Such were the deeds of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he won a name alongside the three mighty warriors. He was honored above the Thirty, but he did not reach the rank of the Three. And David put him in charge of his bodyguard.

The mighty warriors of the army were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem,

Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite,

Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Anathothite,

Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite,

Maharai the Netophathite, Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite,

Ithai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the Benjaminites, Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hurai from the ravines of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,

Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite,

the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shagee the Hararite,

Ahiam son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal son of Ur,

Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,

Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai son of Ezbai,

Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar son of Hagri,

Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah,

Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,

Uriah the Hittite, Zabad son of Ahlai,

Adina son of Shiza the Reubenite, a chief of the Reubenites, and thirty with him,

Hanan son of Maacah, Joshaphat the Mithnite,

Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite,

Jediael son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite,

Eliel the Mahavite, Jeribai and Joshaviah the sons of Elnaam, Ithmah the Moabite, Eliel, Obed and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 12
fields.body_html:
Those who joined David at Ziklag

These are the men who came to David at Ziklag while he still could not move about freely because of Saul son of Kish. They were among the warriors who helped him in battle. They were armed with bows, and they could sling stones and shoot arrows with either the right hand or the left. They were kinsmen of Saul from Benjamin. Their chief was Ahiezer, and next came Joash, both sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite. There were also Jeziel and Pelet the sons of Azmaveth, and Beracah and Jehu the Anathothite. Ishmaiah the Gibeonite was a mighty warrior among the Thirty and a leader over the Thirty. With them were Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan and Jozabad the Gederathite. Also with them were Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah and Shephatiah the Haruphite. Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer and Jashobeam, who were Korahites, were there too. So did Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham from Gedor. Some Gadites broke away and went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness. They were mighty warriors, trained soldiers ready for battle, skilled with shield and spear. Their faces were the faces of lions, and on the mountains they ran as swiftly as gazelles.

Ezer was the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third, Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth, Attai sixth, Eliel seventh, Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth, Jeremiah tenth and Machbannai eleventh. These Gadites were army officers. The least of them could stand against a hundred, and the greatest against a thousand. These men crossed the Jordan in the first month, while the river was flooding over all its banks, and they put to flight everyone in the valleys, east and west.

Some men of Benjamin and Judah also came to David at the stronghold. David went out to meet them and said to them, “If you have come to me in peace to help me, then my heart is one with yours. But if you are here to betray me to my enemies, though I have done no wrong, may the God of our ancestors see it and rebuke you.”

Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the Thirty, and he said,
“We are yours, David! We are with you, son of Jesse!
Peace, peace to you, and peace to whoever helps you,
for your God helps you.”
So David welcomed them and made them leaders of his band.

Some men of Manasseh also went over to David when he came with the Philistines to fight against Saul. But David and his men did not help the Philistines, because the rulers of the Philistines talked it over and sent him away. “He will go back to his master Saul,” they said, “and it will cost us our heads.” As he went back to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh went over to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu and Zillethai, commanders of thousands in Manasseh. They helped David against the band of raiders, for all of them were mighty warriors, and they became commanders in the army. Day after day men came to help David, until he had a great army, like the army of God.

The troops who came to David at Hebron

These are the counts of the divisions armed for war that came to Hebron, to David, to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, as the LORD had said.

From Judah: men carrying shield and spear, 6,800 armed for war.

From Simeon: mighty warriors ready for war, 7,100.

From Levi: 4,600.

Jehoiada was leader of the house of Aaron, and 3,700 came with him.

There was also Zadok, a young man and a mighty warrior, with twenty-two commanders from his father’s family.

From Benjamin, Saul’s own kinsmen: 3,000. Until then most of them had stayed loyal to the house of Saul.

From Ephraim: 20,800 mighty warriors, men famous in their ancestral families.

From the half-tribe of Manasseh: 18,000, who had been named one by one to come and make David king.

From Issachar: 200 chiefs, men with insight into the times, who knew what Israel ought to do, and all their kinsmen took orders from them.

From Zebulun: 50,000 men ready for service in the army, drawn up for battle with every kind of weapon, who came to help with hearts that were not divided.

From Naphtali: 1,000 commanders, and with them 37,000 men carrying shield and spear.

From Dan: 28,600 men drawn up for battle.

From Asher: 40,000 men ready for service in the army, to be drawn up for battle.

From across the Jordan, from Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh: 120,000 men with every kind of weapon for battle. All these fighting men, drawn up in battle order, came to Hebron with an undivided heart to make David king over all Israel. All the rest of Israel too were of one mind to make David king. They stayed there with David for three days, eating and drinking, because their kinsmen had provided for them. Their neighbors too, from as far away as Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali, brought food on donkeys, camels, mules and oxen: plenty of flour, fig cakes, raisin cakes, wine, oil, cattle and sheep. For there was joy in Israel.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 13
fields.body_html:
David sets out to bring up the ark

David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every one of the leaders. Then David said to the whole assembly of Israel, “If you approve, and if this comes from the LORD our God, let us send out in every direction to our fellow Israelites who remain in all the territories of Israel, and to the priests and the Levites with them in the towns where they have their pasturelands, so that they may gather to us. Then let us bring the ark of our God back to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul.” The whole assembly agreed to do this, because the plan seemed right to all the people. So David assembled all Israel, from the Shihor of Egypt as far as Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim. David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim, which belongs to Judah, to bring the ark of God up from there, the ark of the LORD who sits enthroned on the cherubim, the ark which is called by his name. They carried the ark of God on a new cart from Abinadab’s house, while Uzzah and Ahio drove the cart. David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs and with lyres, harps, tambourines, cymbals and trumpets. When they arrived at the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen had stumbled. Then the anger of the LORD blazed against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he had put out his hand to the ark. He died there before God. David was angry because the LORD had burst out against Uzzah, and he named that place Perez-uzzah, a name it still has to this day. David was afraid of God that day, and he said, “How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?” So David did not take the ark into the city of David to be with him. Instead he turned aside and took it to the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. The ark of God stayed for three months with the household of Obed-Edom in his house, and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom’s household and everything he had.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 14
fields.body_html:
David’s kingdom is established

Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, with cedar logs, stonemasons and woodworkers, to build him a palace. Then David knew that the LORD had made him secure as king over Israel, and had raised his kingdom very high for the sake of his people Israel.

In Jerusalem David took more wives, and became the father of more sons and daughters. The names of the children born to him in Jerusalem are these: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet. News reached the Philistines that David had been anointed king over all Israel, so the whole Philistine force went up to hunt for him. But David heard of it and went out to face them. Now the Philistines had come and made a raid on the Valley of Rephaim. So David inquired of God, “Am I to go up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?” The LORD answered him, “Go up, and I will hand them over to you.” So they went up to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. He said, “God has burst through my enemies by my hand, like water breaking through.” That is why that place was named Baal-perazim. The Philistines left their gods behind there, and at David’s command they were burned up.

Another victory over the Philistines

Once again the Philistines made a raid on the valley. When David inquired of God again, God answered him, “Do not go up after them. Circle away from them and attack them opposite the balsam trees. The moment you hear the sound of marching along the tops of the balsam trees, go out to battle, for God has gone out ahead of you to strike down the Philistine army.” David did exactly what God had commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army all the way from Gibeon to Gezer. So David’s fame spread through every land, and the LORD made all the nations dread him.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 15
fields.body_html:
Preparing to bring the ark to Jerusalem

David built houses for himself in the city of David. He also prepared a place for the ark of God, and he pitched a tent for it. Then David said, “No one may carry the ark of God except the Levites, for the LORD chose them to carry the ark of the LORD and to serve him forever.”

David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring the ark of the LORD up to the place he had prepared for it. David gathered the sons of Aaron and the Levites. From the descendants of Kohath: Uriel the chief, and 120 of his relatives.

From the descendants of Merari: Asaiah the chief, and 220 of his relatives.

From the descendants of Gershom: Joel the chief, and 130 of his relatives.

From the descendants of Elizaphan: Shemaiah the chief, and 200 of his relatives.

From the descendants of Hebron: Eliel the chief, and eighty of his relatives.

From the descendants of Uzziel: Amminadab the chief, and 112 of his relatives.

Then David summoned Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel and Amminadab. He said to them, “You are the heads of the Levite families. Consecrate yourselves, you and your relatives, and bring the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, up to the place I have prepared for it. It was because you did not carry it the first time that the LORD our God burst out against us, since we did not seek him as the rule required.” So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves in order to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel. The Levites carried the ark of God with the poles on their shoulders, as Moses had commanded by the word of the LORD.

The Levite singers and musicians

David also told the chiefs of the Levites to appoint some of their relatives as singers, with musical instruments, harps, lyres and cymbals, to play loudly and raise sounds of joy.

So the Levites appointed Heman son of Joel; from his relatives, Asaph son of Berechiah; and from their relatives the descendants of Merari, Ethan son of Kushaiah. With them were their relatives of the second rank: Zechariah, Ben, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-Edom and Jeiel. The singers Heman, Asaph and Ethan were to play bronze cymbals loudly. Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah and Benaiah were to play harps, on alamoth. Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, Jeiel and Azaziah were to lead with lyres, on the sheminith. Chenaniah, the chief of the Levites in charge of the music, directed the music, because he was skilled at it. Berechiah and Elkanah were gatekeepers for the ark. Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, who were priests, were to sound the trumpets in front of the ark of God. Obed-Edom and Jehiah were gatekeepers for the ark as well. So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD up from the house of Obed-Edom with rejoicing.

The ark comes to Jerusalem

When God helped the Levites carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they offered seven bulls and seven rams in sacrifice. David was dressed in a robe of fine linen, and so were all the Levites carrying the ark, the singers and Chenaniah, who led the music of the singers. David also wore a linen ephod. So all Israel brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD up with loud shouts of joy and the sound of the ram’s horn, with trumpets and cymbals, and with the loud music of harps and lyres. As the ark of the covenant of the LORD was coming into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked down from the window. She saw King David dancing and celebrating, and in her heart she despised him.

fields.title: 1 Chronicles 16
fields.body_html:
The ark in its tent

They carried the ark of God in and set it within the tent David had pitched for it. Then they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God. When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he pronounced a blessing on the people in the name of the LORD. He also handed out food to every person in Israel, both men and women: a loaf of bread, a cake of dates and a cake of raisins for each one. He appointed some of the Levites to serve before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel.

Asaph was the leader, and next to him was Zechariah. Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-Edom and Jeiel played harps and lyres, and Asaph sounded the cymbals. The priests Benaiah and Jahaziel blew trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God. It was on that day that David first put Asaph and his fellow Levites in charge of giving thanks to the LORD:

David’s song of thanks

Thank the LORD and call on his name;
tell every people what he has done.
Sing to him, play and sing his praise;
talk of all the wonderful things he has done.
Take pride in his holy name;
let all who look to the LORD be glad at heart.
Turn to the LORD and to his strength;
come into his presence again and again.
Call to mind the wonders he has worked,
his signs, and the verdicts he spoke,
you descendants of his servant Israel,
you children of Jacob, the ones he chose.
He, the LORD, is our God;
his rulings reach the whole earth.
Keep his covenant in mind forever,
the promise he laid down for a thousand generations,
the covenant he made with Abraham,
the oath he swore to Isaac,
and he set it in place for Jacob as a decree,
for Israel as a covenant that lasts forever,
saying, “The land of Canaan I give to you,
a share marked out for you to inherit.”
When you were only a handful of people,
a few outsiders living in that land,
wandering from one nation to the next,
from one kingdom to another people,
he let no one do them wrong,
and he took kings to task over them:
“Do not lay a hand on my anointed ones;
do not hurt my prophets.”

All the earth, sing to the LORD!
Day after day announce the good news of how he saves.
Tell the nations of his glory,
and all the peoples of the wonders he has done.
For the LORD is great and worthy of the highest praise;
he must be revered above every god.
For every god the peoples serve is a mere nothing, an idol,
but it was the LORD who made the heavens.
Splendor and majesty stand in his presence;
strength and joy fill the place where he dwells.
Give the LORD what is due, you families of the nations;
give the LORD glory and might.
Give the LORD the glory his name deserves;
bring a gift and come into his presence;
bow low before the LORD in holy splendor.
Tremble in his presence, all the earth!
The world stands firm; nothing can make it totter.
Let the heavens be full of joy and the earth be glad;
let it be told among the nations, “The LORD is King!”
Let the sea thunder with all that lives in it;
let the fields and everything in them celebrate.
Then the trees of the woods will cry out with joy
in the presence of the LORD, for he is on the way to judge the earth.
Give the LORD thanks, for he is good;
his loyal love lasts forever.
Say also, “Rescue us, God our Savior;
gather us and deliver us from among the nations,
so that we may thank your holy name and make our boast in praising you.”
